items.title: Austria May Strip Former Foreign Minister Karin Kneissl of Citizenship
items.summary: The onetime foreign minister, Karin Kneissl, has lauded her new home for its “genuine freedom” and used it as a perch to attack her old one.
items.full_text: The Austrian authorities have taken initial steps to revoke the citizenship of a former foreign minister who moved to Russia — a country she has lauded for its “genuine freedom” — and who has repeatedly denigrated Austria while echoing Kremlin-friendly talking points. Karin Kneissl made international headlines when she danced with President Vladimir Putin of Russia at her wedding in 2018, when she was her nation’s top diplomat. Since then, she has angered many of her compatriots with regular barbs against her country of birth and its citizens. That the Austrian state would even consider the extraordinary step of revoking her citizenship reflects a national weariness about the former foreign minister. It follows a prolonged national debate over whether Ms. Kneissl retained the right to remain Austrian after — both physically and by all appearances ideologically — turning her back on her homeland. Ms. Kneissl, who served as foreign minister from 2017 to 2019, made her very public move to Russia in 2023, a year after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. She was hired to run a think tank in St. Petersburg. Over the years, Ms. Kneissl, 61, seems to have taken pleasure in denigrating Austrians in interviews with Russian-friendly media. Earlier this year, for example, she repeated her claim that Hitler, who was born in Austria, was typically Austrian. She also said that her countrymen had acted like hyenas toward her. Such comments served to bolster a push to strip her of her citizenship. The initiative has been led by the liberal party NEOS, which is run by the current foreign minister, Beate Meinl-Reisinger. “Why does Kneissl continue to appear prominently as Austria’s former foreign minister when she so obviously despises and hates our country?” Yannick Shetty, a NEOS member of the Austrian Parliament, asked in January in response to Ms. Kneissl’s remarks. On Monday, officials in Vienna confirmed that an inquiry into the former minister had been launched. They said they were looking at whether she had obtained a second citizenship and whether her conduct significantly harmed “the interests or reputation of the Republic.” It remains unclear if the inquiry will actually lead to the revocation of her citizenship and, if so, how long it might take. Ms. Kneissl was proposed for the post of foreign minister in 2017 by the far-right Freedom Party of Austria, though she was never a member of that party. After leaving Austria in 2020, she went to France and Lebanon before moving to a little village southeast of Moscow in the heartland of Russia. On Monday, Ms. Kneissl said she knew that steps were being taken to revoke her citizenship. In comments reported by the Russian state news agency Tass, she said that if Austria moved forward with the plan, she would end up stateless and need to apply for travel documents from the United Nations.

items.title: Airstrikes on Iran Missile Sites May Shed Light on Justification for Dams
items.summary: Environmentalists have long puzzled over a wide network of water projects lacking any obvious justification. Then their areas were targeted in airstrikes.
items.full_text: Environmentalists have long been mystified by the significant proliferation of dams and water transfer projects like pipelines and tunnels across Iran, especially in regions that had no apparent need for them. Some analysts think they now know the answer after U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on concealed Iranian missile sites this year targeted many of the same areas. These analysts have concluded that the water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup. Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive. Nima Shokri, an expert on water security, and his team at the Hamburg University of Technology, in Germany, had for years tracked an unusually high number of dams across Iran — at least 533 of them, among the most of any country in the region. “It was always puzzling to me,” he said. “Why were they building so many dams?” In the spring, Dr. Shokri was perusing news about the war in his home country when he came across a map plotting airstrikes that had targeted suspected military sites. The pattern — a semicircle of dots from north to south — nearly matched that of his own map marking the locations of dams. His old question, he said, was superseded by a new one: “Why does it seem that wherever we have dams, there is a missile strike close by?” Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: 10 Numbers That Might Change How You See Asia
items.summary: From semiconductor dominance to new power grids, defense deals and K-pop, the region — beyond China — is becoming increasingly interconnected and self-reliant.
items.full_text: President Trump’s trip to Asia this week will largely be seen as a test of American power in the main region where the United States and China compete for influence. His meetings in Manila and Shenzhen, China, will be scrutinized for shifts on trade and security. Deals he might strike with Beijing — plus a gathering with President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia — will put the world’s great-power contest on display, as all three seek to show strength. But Asia is not just a theater of competition. Many countries in the region have become wealthier, more technologically advanced and increasingly interconnected . Especially now, as China’s military becomes more threatening and the United States less reliable, they are hedging against greatness and relying more on neighbors. Asian students and workers are moving to neighboring states. Countries with expanding defense industries are selling weapons to new partners. Nations that compete for high-tech investment are even making plans to cooperate on energy and cybersecurity . “They’re all looking at what more they can do together when the great powers are behaving so badly,” said Ted Osius, a former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam and adjunct professor of geopolitics at Fulbright University in Ho Chi Minh City. “If you’re a middle power, you’re thinking ‘I need more options.’” Here are a few numbers that provide a sense of what the region contributes to the global economy, and how its nations are becoming more bound together to shape the world. items.title: Pope Endures Grueling Travel in South America Weeks After Surgery
items.summary: When doctors operated on Pope Leo XIV’s lung in October, some wondered if he’d postpone a long-planned trip to South America. It’s gone well so far.
items.full_text: Flying with Pope Leo XIV over the Andes, halfway through the pontiff’s 12-day trip to South America, the journalists traveling at the back of the plane suspected something was amiss. They had expected the pope to come out from behind the business-class curtain and take questions, as he had on previous papal flights. Instead, Vatican officials abruptly told the press corps that the pope would not be speaking with them on the nearly five-hour flight from Argentina to Peru. Was the pope, who had been diagnosed with lung cancer less than a month earlier, feeling ill? Was he too exhausted to talk? Was he taking a nap? “It’s evident he’s well,” said Maria Montserrat Alvarado, who heads the Vatican’s communications department, when asked why the pope wasn’t taking questions. “He’s running circles around us.” It was perhaps inevitable that Leo’s every action on this journey, so soon after surgery to remove a lobe of his right lung, would be scrutinized for signs of fatigue or illness, particularly as the Vatican is not known for its transparency . The three-country trip, which began in Uruguay and concludes in Peru on Monday, involves a grueling schedule of 12 flights, two helicopter rides, nine Masses, 36 speeches and numerous meetings with local bishops and community members. items.title: Five European Countries Plan to Deport Migrants to Rwanda
items.summary: Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark are seeking to establish a hub for rejected asylum seekers. Here’s what to know about their effort.
items.full_text: Five European countries announced a plan on Monday that would send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda , an experiment that comes as governments across the continent toughen their stances on migration. The joint push from Germany, Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece was pitched as a way to handle migrants who had no right to stay in Europe but who, for one reason or another, could not or would not return to their home countries. The project, which is not yet finalized, shows how European leaders’ stance on migration has hardened since the arrivals of 2015-16, when countries like Germany admitted more than a million asylum seekers. With far-right groups like the Alternative for Germany rising in popularity, centrist leaders have gradually taken a less welcoming stance. “For me, today marks a crucial step toward a new migration system,” Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister of Denmark, said at a news conference on Monday. The pilot project is expected to start on a small scale, with perhaps 100 or 200 deportees. Critics are already worried both about the idea of sending people to a nation to which they have no connection, and about the risk that human rights will not be sufficiently protected in Rwanda. Why Rwanda? The country has a history of courting migration-related deals. Britain developed a plan to send asylum seekers there in 2022, though judges in London ultimately ruled the effort unlawful and it was later abandoned. The United States has recently deported people to Rwanda. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Bahrain Convicts Dozens of Shiite Clerics in Sweeping Terrorism Trial
items.summary: The defendants were accused of colluding with Iran. Rights groups said the case was marred by torture allegations and raised concerns about religious persecution.
items.full_text: Bahrain sentenced dozens of Shiite Muslim clerics and other religious figures to life in prison on terrorism charges on Monday, accusing them of colluding with Iran against the Bahraini government. The convictions underscored rising sectarian and political tensions in Bahrain, a Gulf Arab country, amid the U.S.-Israeli war on Shiite-led Iran. Human rights groups had denounced the mass trial , saying that it was marred by allegations of torture and coerced confessions. A lawyer for several of the defendants, speaking on condition of anonymity out of fear of retribution from Bahrain’s authoritarian government, said that all of them had pleaded not guilty. He described the trial as farcical, saying that lawyers had been deprived of basic information about the charges against their clients. When asked about those claims, the Bahraini government said in a statement that all of the defendants had been “afforded their full legal rights and safeguards, including the right of defense,” and that complaints of mistreatment would be referred for investigation. “This case was about criminal conduct, not faith or belief,” the government added. The Bahraini authorities had accused the defendants of forming a “terrorist group” linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps of Iran. According to a statement from the Bahraini public prosecution department, published by the state news agency, the defendants had worked to undermine the Bahraini government, and the group’s leaders had received “assignments and instructions” from Iranian officials. “They had also sought to change the system of government by force and unlawful means through incitement to commit terrorist acts, acts of rioting and sabotage,” the statement added. items.title: U.N. Starts Uncertain Effort to Regulate Lethal Autonomous Weapons
items.summary: Delegates met in Geneva to discuss guardrails for such systems even as their development grows. Russia and the United States have resisted the efforts.
items.full_text: Global efforts to limit the use of lethal autonomous weapons reached a crossroads this week as countries gathered to decide whether to negotiate binding restrictions on the technology, despite strong resistance from the United States and Russia. Delegates of 128 states met at the United Nations in Geneva on Monday for a weeklong conference to determine whether to draft a treaty that would ban lethal autonomous weapons and require meaningful human control of such systems. “The longer the international community waits, the more difficult it will become to establish meaningful safeguards — and it may be too late,” Volker Türk, the U.N. human rights chief, said before the conference. Artificial intelligence and its military uses are developing at breakneck speed, as seen on the battlefields of Ukraine and the Middle East . That has deepened international alarm and prompted calls for action by many countries, global leaders and activist groups, even as top military powers balk at attempts to curb their ability to develop new weapons. “Decisions affecting human life, freedom and the use of force must always remain subject to effective, informed and responsible human oversight,” Pope Leo XIV said in a statement last month that urged those at the Geneva conference to take “concrete “steps” to ban lethal autonomous weapons. Artificial intelligence, he said, “must be ‘disarmed.’” Russia and Ukraine have already deployed fully autonomous drones to carry out attacks. Disarmament experts fear that the low cost and easy availability of such technology could lead to its rapid spread to law enforcement, nonstate armed groups and organized crime. items.title: Winter Nightmare Looms Early in Ukraine as Russia Strikes Relentlessly
items.summary: Even as it talks peace, Russia has opened a bombing campaign intended to strip Kyiv and other cities of heat, running water and sanitation this winter.
items.full_text: When American-led talks to end the war in Ukraine resumed last week in Abu Dhabi , the overriding question was whether Russia intended to give any ground after a nine-month lull in negotiations. But Russian missiles and drones had already done the talking for Moscow, analysts said . Weeks earlier than expected, Russia has opened an intense bombing campaign against the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainians alive and functioning in the winter. Daily waves of strikes against Ukraine’s energy system have raised fears that the capital, Kyiv, a city of three million people, could become all but uninhabitable in the coming months. In the Abu Dhabi talks, an emboldened Russia outlined hard-line demands that stood little chance of gaining acceptance by Ukraine and its European allies. That unbending stance indicated that Russia had no real interest in discussing peace now, because Moscow believes that the winter bombing campaign will strengthen its negotiating position entering the spring. “They want to come to the table holding our energy system hostage,” President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said after a recent Russian attack. The Abu Dhabi talks will be followed by a meeting on Thursday between President Trump, President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, at a summit in Shenzhen, China. It was unclear whether the three leaders would discuss the war in Ukraine. Assaulting infrastructure has become Moscow’s strategy for victory as it has failed for nearly five years to achieve its major objectives in Ukraine. While Russia has tried each winter to knock out the country’s power system and freeze its people into submission, Ukrainian cities are now in their most precarious position of the war. The grid is more fragile after years of strikes, and the Ukrainian military is struggling to protect the system because of dwindling air defenses. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Trump’s Asia Trip Will Bring Him to the Table With Xi and Putin: What to Know
items.summary: President Trump will also meet with regional leaders, including Australia’s prime minister, who said “we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts.”
items.full_text: President Trump sets off this week for meetings in Asia that will culminate in a summit with two strongmen he has often praised: President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. It will be the first time the three men, who command the world’s largest nuclear arsenals, will have sat down together. Mr. Trump plans to discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world and the war against Iran, according to a White House spokeswoman. He is not expected to bring up Russia’s war with Ukraine. Mr. Trump will travel first to Manila, then to southern China, and will meet with regional leaders confronting an array of uncertainties. Those include the course of the war between the United States and Iran, high energy prices and mounting concern over the risks of artificial intelligence. For Mr. Trump, the trip will be a pivot to foreign policy and relationships after American voters delivered a swift rebuke to his party in the midterm elections. His trip also comes as his administration faces scrutiny over a scandal involving the former chief executive of Nvidia, the tech giant, which has raised questions about Chinese espionage and American tech exports. Echoes of Yalta The highlight of Mr. Trump’s trip is expected to be his meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin on Thursday in China. The prospect of their summit has drawn comparisons to the 1945 conference in the Crimean city of Yalta, where the leaders of the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain met to decide the shape of postwar Europe. items.title: South Korea to Examine How K-Pop Industry Treats Underage Performers
items.summary: The announcement came after a New York Times investigation about the restrictive contracts of the group NewJeans, signed when its members were 14 to 17.
items.full_text: South Korea’s government is planning to study how the K-pop industry treats underage performers, who are central to the industry, and to re-examine the standard template for contracts it released nearly two decades ago. The Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism will start an industrywide survey sometime next year, a ministry official said in a telephone interview on Monday. The government already studies the K-pop industry, checking whether record companies follow its standard contract and how much money is invested in training young stars. The new effort will focus specifically on how underage artists are treated, but its methodology, scope and exact timeline have not been decided on. The announcement came just over a week after The New York Times published an investigation into the record contracts signed by the members of NewJeans, one of K-pop’s biggest girl groups, when they were ages 14 to 17. The investigation found that the contracts removed language included in the government template that guarantees rights for minors, such as the rights to education and sleep. It was a rare look into the business of K-pop, which has long been dogged by allegations of exploitation . Record companies recruit children who are aspiring stars, put them through years of intensive training and then often bill them for those costs. Several stars have died by suicide . Two years ago, NewJeans tried to quit their label in a dispute that turned into one of K-pop’s most public fights, with the members saying they had been mistreated. A court later held them to the contracts they had signed, which run until 2029. The Seoul Broadcasting System reported the ministry’s plan earlier. In 2009 , after a boy band sued its label over restrictive work agreements, the authorities created a standard contract. It outlined protections such as capping agreements at seven years, taking into consideration an artist’s physical and mental well-being and transferring trademark rights to the artist after the terms end. The template has been amended several times over the years but still largely remains legally nonbinding. Record companies often alter clauses and add their own conditions. Some do not use the template at all, a government survey found.

items.title: Pilots Kept Contact With Controllers During Nationwide Halt to Flights
items.summary: Pilots were generally able to maintain contact with air traffic controllers and airline staff on the ground despite an outage that caused a nearly five-hour halt to departures.
items.full_text: Pilots were able to maintain communications with air traffic controllers and airline dispatchers during the nationwide halt to most departing flights imposed by federal officials for nearly five hours on Friday. A representative of the union that represents about 17,000 pilots at American Airlines said on Monday that it had received no reports of crews losing radio contact with controllers. Some pilots noticed radio static, but that isn’t uncommon, said Dennis Tajer, a spokesman for the union, the Allied Pilots Association. Even so, the union said it supported the hourslong ground stop called by the Federal Aviation Administration, a part of the Department of Transportation. “Just because the national shutdown happened without incident, let that not be the catalyst for doubting if the right call was made,” said Mr. Tajer, who is a Boeing 737 captain and was stranded near Newark Liberty International Airport on Friday night. “You just don’t know what would have happened had you said, ‘Well, let’s take a chance and see.’” Southwest Airlines dispatchers, who help to plan and guide the carrier’s flights, also reported no disruption of direct communications or data before the ground stop was ordered. “Dispatchers did not experience any loss of communication with our flight crews or F.A.A. control facilities, and our tools and data feeds did not show any signs of disruption,” said Kevin Thurston, the president of Transport Workers Union Local 550, the union that represents dispatchers and meteorologists at the airline. The F.A.A. has said that the technical outage was intermittent and not a blackout, noting over the weekend that some radio frequencies and radar feeds remained reliable. The agency said the problem began when data began flooding an agency telecommunications network. An initial investigation identified two possible sources: a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Ark. An investigation is ongoing. “Throughout the disruption, certain radio frequencies and radar feeds remained operational, allowing air traffic controllers to maintain communication with and track aircraft,” the agency said in a statement. Even if primary communications had gone dark, aircraft are equipped with backups. Pilots can use emergency frequencies to speak with nearby planes and ground facilities. Aviation professionals can also use other tools to communicate with dispatchers, including text-based systems. “We have plenty of knives in our boot,” said Mr. Tajer. “It doesn’t mean we want to use them.”

items.title: United Airlines Flights Resume After ‘Widespread System Outage’
items.summary: The brief disruption, after a nationwide ground stop last week, added to concerns about air travel ahead of a busy Thanksgiving travel period.
items.full_text: United Airlines said it had resolved a “widespread system outage” that grounded planes and briefly stranded passengers on Monday, unnerving travelers as the nation’s aviation system was recovering from the ground stoppage that paralyzed air traffic late last week. The airline said that “while some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” referring to its regional network of smaller carriers that operate shorter flights on United’s behalf. The outage was reported just before 5 p.m. Eastern time and was resolved after about an hour. In an earlier statement announcing the disruption, the airline said that it was “troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights but that there was “no impact on flights in progress.” United did not immediately provide additional details about the outage, which was reported just days before millions of Americans, many of them jittery about delays and other problems with air travel, will begin traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday. People have been unnerved by a series of technical outages that have disrupted their daily lives. Last week, many Microsoft systems went down, bringing email, work messaging platforms and other corporate systems to a halt. Then there was the five-hour national halt to all flights caused by a seemingly minor upgrade to the communications system used by air traffic controllers. And on Monday, JPMorgan Chase said a “ software bug ” had impeded its ability to process some financial transactions. Among the passengers who were delayed by the United outage on Monday was Craig Gruen, 43, who was flying from Charleston, S.C., to Denver. As his plane sat on the tarmac, he said the captain told passengers that the crew could not verify the plane’s weight through United’s management system. While Mr. Gruen was on the phone with a New York Times reporter, the captain said over the plane’s intercom that United was connecting its narrow-body planes to an older system to verify weight information, so the flight could be cleared for takeoff. Mr. Gruen said was not eager to go on future trips because he doesn’t want to deal with the hassle. “When technology continuously fails, I’m losing trust in the systems,” he said. Airlines sometimes experience short-lived technical disruptions and can recover quickly if the problem is swiftly addressed. But a lengthy outage can become destabilizing as pilots and flight attendants reach legal working limits and delays and cancellations ripple throughout a carrier’s network. This is a developing story.

items.title: Bessent Takes Hawkish Turn in White House Debate on China
items.summary: The Treasury secretary who sought to de-escalate tariff wars is taking a tougher approach to exports of sensitive U.S. technology.
items.full_text: President Trump heads to Asia on Monday for high-stakes meetings with foreign leaders aimed at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine and smoothing over trade frictions with China. But the most tense meeting could take place aboard Air Force One. Sequestered together on the journey across the world will be Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, whose long-running rivalry has recently spilled into the open. Mr. Lutnick is under fire for slow-walking several measures aimed at clamping down on the supply of Nvidia chips to foreign data centers that serve Chinese clients. The controversy has put Mr. Lutnick at odds with Mr. Bessent, who has increasingly taken a hard line on China. While Mr. Lutnick has pushed for policies more favorable to Nvidia, Mr. Bessent has played the foil, going so far as to call for a dramatic shake-up of the company’s leadership. The Treasury secretary traditionally manages America’s economic relationship with China. After spending much of last year trying to de-escalate tension between the world’s two largest economies over tariffs, Mr. Bessent has taken a more hawkish stance this year amid growing concern over the artificial intelligence race with China and risks that rogue Chinese A.I. technology could pose to the U.S. economy. The internal clash over China policy has echoes of Mr. Trump’s first term, when the president’s economic advisers regularly argued about how forcefully to confront China over its trade practices. After Mr. Trump imposed steep tariffs on Chinese imports last year, Mr. Bessent called for de-escalation and helped broker a trade truce that stabilized the global economy. But in recent months, the Trump administration has been frustrated that China has not lived up to its commitments for purchases of American farm products and to accelerate exports of its critical minerals, which are needed for making high-tech electronics and military equipment. items.title: Trump Nominates Budget Deputy for Nonpartisan Federal Watchdog Role
items.summary: The move could put a top administration official in charge of an oversight agency that has faulted the White House for past violations of the law.
items.full_text: President Trump on Monday nominated Eric M. Ueland, a top deputy at the White House budget office, to serve as the nation’s comptroller general, a move that could hand control of a nonpartisan federal watchdog to one of the administration’s political allies. If confirmed by the Senate, Mr. Ueland would assume the leadership of the Government Accountability Office, an agency whose responsibilities include monitoring federal spending, identifying government waste and ensuring that the executive branch complies with the wishes of Congress. The post carries a 15-year term. The selection of Mr. Ueland quickly evoked furious opposition from top congressional Democrats, who accused Mr. Trump of trying to neuter legislative oversight just weeks before Republicans are set to surrender control of Congress. Mr. Ueland currently serves under Russell T. Vought, the director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, which has worked on behalf of Mr. Trump to block billions of dollars in spending and fire droves of civil workers, often without the explicit approval of Congress. Frequently, the office known as G.A.O. has found some of those activities to be illegal. The problems date back to the president’s first term, when the accountability office concluded in 2020 that the White House had wrongly withheld nearly $400 million in military assistance to Ukraine. Congressional Democrats would later cite that finding when they commenced a push to impeach Mr. Trump. But the violations have continued into Mr. Trump’s second stint in office. Repeatedly, the G.A.O. has found that the budget office, where Mr. Ueland is deputy director, has illegally withheld congressionally enacted funds in spite of laws that prohibit the practice, which is known as impoundment Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Fed Chairman Highlights Economic Uncertainty of A.I. Boom
items.summary: Kevin M. Warsh, chairman of the Federal Reserve, has assigned a task force to explore how productivity gains tied to new technologies could impact the labor market.
items.full_text: Kevin M. Warsh on Monday underscored how uncertain the artificial intelligence boom could be for the economy, highlighting the potential for increased productivity and growth as well as job losses and disappointing stock market returns. Mr. Warsh’s remarks kicked off a conference at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco that homed in on the work of a task force he established to examine how productivity gains might affect the labor market . It is one of five groups that Mr. Warsh created to look into issues that he has said are central to monetary policy. Mr. Warsh said that the Fed was modeling scenarios related to how A.I. might impact the economy . Productivity growth had in recent months been “reasonably strong,” he noted, but it “hasn’t yet broken out definitively and structurally to the upside.” Under the most positive circumstances, the technology could lead “to an increase in productivity and economic gains that are shared broadly ​across labor and the owners of capital,” Mr. Warsh said. In that case, economic growth would rise “persistently above its long-run average” and the unemployment rate would remain steady. In a gloomier case, Mr. Warsh warned of “substantial labor market disruption” in which jobs are “displaced, rather than complemented” by A.I. In that scenario, the likely outcome would be higher growth but rising unemployment. Lastly, Mr. Warsh raised the prospect that A.I. returns could disappoint relative to the enormous investment that has flooded into the technology , which has pushed up stock valuations and helped to power consumer spending. At risk in that scenario is an economic slowdown as the broader market falls. Productivity gains are unlikely to accrue against that backdrop, he said. items.title: Willie Geist Is Leaving ‘Morning Joe’ After Nearly 20 Years
items.summary: He will take on an expanded role at NBC News, where he has been the host of the Sunday edition of the “Today” show since 2016.
items.full_text: Willie Geist, who has been a host of the “Morning Joe” cable news franchise for nearly two decades, said on Monday that he will leave the show at the end of the year to take on an expanded role with NBC News. Mr. Geist framed his departure as inevitable, as he had been splitting his work life between two networks: MS NOW, the home of “Morning Joe,” and NBC, where he hosts the Sunday edition of the “Today” show and appears in other capacities on the morning program. That arrangement was easier to manage when the networks were owned by the same parent company, Comcast, and were both operating out of studios at 30 Rockefeller Plaza in Manhattan. MS NOW, then known as MSNBC, was among the cable channels once part of the NBCUniversal TV empire that were spun off under an arrangement formalized earlier this year . NBC said on Monday that Mr. Geist had been the only on-air employee working for both NBC News and MS NOW since the separation. “It was never intended to last forever,” Mr. Geist said on Monday’s episode of “Morning Joe.” He said he was leaving “with a very heavy heart, heavy with memories and experiences and friends and family.” He also addressed his co-hosts, Joe Scarborough and Mika Brzezinski, with whom he had worked since the show premiered in April 2007. “A run that’s lasted nearly 20 years beside the two of you,” he said, had been “the joy of a lifetime, the job of a lifetime.” Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Elon Musk Wants to Merge Tesla and SpaceX. Their Businesses Already Overlap.
items.summary: For years, engineers have shuffled between Tesla and SpaceX, and the companies have worked on major projects together.
items.full_text: Nearly a decade ago, Elon Musk gave Tesla’s design team an unusual assignment: Build a sports car that can fly. Mr. Musk brought in a small team of engineers from SpaceX, his rocket company, to lend a hand. Led by Bill Riley, SpaceX’s executive overseeing engineering on the rocket intended to land NASA astronauts on the moon, the team juggled their day jobs with outfitting a Roadster sports car with cold-gas thrusters, a technology more commonly found in rockets that has enough force to burst a human eardrum, according to three people familiar with the project. This year, as engineers from both companies prepared for the car’s debut, they spent months putting it through its paces at SpaceX’s rocket testing facility in McGregor, Texas, the people said. In October, a driverless Roadster did a kick flip in midair, launching off a ramp more than 60 feet high. This is “what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company” Mr. Musk told the crowd. The flying car demonstration offered a rare glimpse into how the world’s richest person has already created unusual cooperations between his two companies — which he now hopes to merge into a conglomerate valued at more than $3 trillion. For years, Mr. Musk has quietly shuffled executives and engineers between Tesla and SpaceX to work on his passion projects, blurring the lines between the two, according to interviews with more than a dozen current and former employees, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential business matters. The arrangements highlight how Mr. Musk treated the huge companies as interchangeable parts of a single empire, long before shareholders have been asked to vote on combining them. items.title: Elon Musk Dreams of Merging Tesla and SpaceX in Move Toward Tech Supremacy
items.summary: The history of the sprawling corporate combinations is rich, colorful and mostly disappointing. Could a SpaceX-Tesla merger be a success story?
items.full_text: No one could accuse Elon Musk of thinking small. And the vision he described last month of merging his two companies SpaceX and Tesla is characteristically ambitious: a digital conglomerate of unprecedented scale, spanning rockets, satellites, electric cars, robots and social media. Mr. Musk is not alone as a digital-age corporate empire builder. Other tech giants are also now sprawling, multi-industry enterprises. Alphabet’s businesses range well beyond Google search and cloud computing to include video streaming, self-driving cars, drone delivery service and drug development. Amazon has e-commerce, cloud computing, video streaming, a movie studio, robots, warehouses and delivery services. But a SpaceX-Tesla merger would eclipse the others in its striking array of different businesses, forming a mega-conglomerate worth about $3.5 trillion. Conglomerates of the past were typically driven by purely financial considerations, like the 1960s merger frenzy on Wall Street, or to diversify a company in order to make it better able to weather economic cycles and international competition, like General Electric. But today’s conglomerate impulse has a different source — a drive for technological supremacy by broadening a corporation’s market reach and gaining an upper hand in the global A.I. race. items.title: Robert Pattinson Named as the Next James Bond
items.summary: The announcement ends years of speculation over who would take over the role after Daniel Craig’s five-film run.
items.full_text: After seven years of rumors, wish lists and wild guesses, Hollywood’s most feverishly followed casting search is over: Amazon MGM Studios has chosen Robert Pattinson to play James Bond. Pattinson, the 40-year-old English actor, will become the seventh man to play 007 in the official 25-film series. Pattinson is known for blockbusters like “Twilight,” “The Batman” and, most recently, “The Odyssey.” “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement,” Pattinson said in a statement. He succeeds Daniel Craig, who announced in 2019 that he would depart the role. Craig’s decision set off a frenzy of speculation among Bond enthusiasts, bookmakers and the British tabloids. Who could be trusted to step into the multibillion-dollar franchise? What kind of Bond would click with a new generation? Should Bond be Black ? Or female ? At various points, the supposed candidates included Idris Elba, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Hardy, Regé-Jean Page, Tom Holland, Jacob Elordi and Theo James. Pattinson was chosen over Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner. The five actors underwent screen tests in London in late October. The auditions involved stunts, dialogue and camera presence; they were overseen by Nina Gold, an Oscar-nominated (“Hamnet”) and Emmy-winning (“Game of Thrones”) casting director. Bond auditions can be revealing: Henry Cavill, who lost the role to Craig in the previous casting search, told Men’s Health in 2019 that he was asked to re-enact a scene in which Sean Connery’s Bond emerged from a bathroom in nothing but a towel. James Bond is one of the most coveted — and unforgiving — roles in moviedom. When Craig was cast in 2005, taking over from Pierce Brosnan, detractors complained that he was too blond, too short and insufficiently suave. Carping fans have long been part of the Bond tradition, but the internet gave them a new megaphone. Craig’s “fleshy” ears and “potato” face were mocked on message boards. One group even created a protest website , CraigNotBond.com. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: American Roosters Fight in the Philippines Despite U.S. Crackdown
items.summary: It’s illegal in the United States to transport game fowl for fighting. But investigators say breeders are sending birds to the Philippines, where cockfighting is legal and lucrative.
items.full_text: Jerry Jalandoni navigated hundreds of chickens running loose on his farm in the Philippines before stopping at a row of tall cages that held his latest acquisitions: a dozen cockfighting roosters from the United States. On top of one cage was a cardboard box, poked with holes that had allowed a hen to breathe during her solitary journey from Texas to Bacolod City. “She’s been through a lot,” Mr. Jalandoni said. The hen arrived alone, he said, because her mate had been held back by exporters wary of attracting the attention of animal rights groups. Such birds come from game fowl breeds developed in the United States that are renowned internationally for their sturdiness and aggression — qualities valued in cockfighting, a legal and highly profitable industry in the Philippines. Those birds were not supposed to be on Mr. Jalandoni’s farm, according to U.S. federal laws. But they are part of a trade in which breeders in the United States send fighting roosters to the Philippines. Cockfighting — the practice of tying metal blades, or gaffs, to the legs of roosters that fight each other to the death — has been illegal in the United States since 2008, when Louisiana became the last state to outlaw it. Transporting animals across state lines or out of the country for the purpose of fighting was banned in 1976 . While the trade has long been an open secret, the channels through which American fighting birds arrive in Asia are drawing fresh scrutiny from U.S. officials.

items.title: How Jensen Huang’s Secret Led to His Downfall at Nvidia
items.summary: Nvidia’s leader said his relationship with a female customer was just about business. But what he was concealing eventually led to his resignation from the company he created.
items.full_text: Jensen Huang was agitated. It was September 2025, and The New York Times had just called his company about a Singaporean data center firm called Megaspeed that had been led by a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, or Huang Le. The Times was reporting that Mr. Huang, the chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, had a close relationship with her. Mr. Huang, who Nvidia employees say could have a volcanic temper, wanted to know what The Times was insinuating. Though he didn’t deny that he knew the woman, he was bothered by the suggestion that they might be close, people familiar with the discussion said. Nvidia mounted an aggressive defense. Madison Huang, Mr. Huang’s daughter who acted as her father’s chief of staff, pressed the company’s communications team to push back forcefully. They also had reinforcements, a crisis communications firm called Heller. They insisted that Mr. Huang and the woman from Megaspeed just had a business relationship. Over the next 13 months, Mr. Huang stuck with his story, even after The Times reported last month that the U.S. had gathered intelligence showing that Ms. Huang was secretly working with China’s top spy agency. But last weekend, facing new revelations about the relationship, Mr. Huang finally came clean to Nvidia’s general counsel. He had been having an affair with the woman, after all, said the people familiar with the discussions. The relationship with the Megaspeed executive wasn’t Mr. Huang’s only secret. On Wednesday, a Times reporter called Mr. Huang to ask him about a second extramarital relationship. This time, it was an affair with an executive who reported to him. items.title: The Jensen Huang Scandal Has Shocked Even Scandal-Prone Silicon Valley
items.summary: As Jensen Huang abruptly departs, the tech community grapples with an eternal question: Why do the smartest and most successful men so often act so stupidly?
items.full_text: Artificial intelligence promises transcendence. We will ditch our tired and inefficient bodies, say farewell to tedious work and trips to the grocery store. The computer will tend to all human needs and solve all human problems. Well, that was the idea. A.I. was supposed to achieve a new level of reality this month with the public sale of shares of Anthropic, one of the two start-ups that have created and defined this young industry. A trillion-dollar company will be born, yielding billionaires galore. A.I. is the biggest Silicon Valley story ever. But last Sunday it was suddenly pushed aside when the chief executive of the company whose chips are literally powering this intelligence revolution confessed to cheating on his wife with a woman, Alice Huang, who U.S. officials believe was spying for China. By Thursday morning he had resigned, something few thought possible just days earlier. The scandal that took down Nvidia chief Jensen Huang is full of implications for national security and the global A.I. boom. Mr. Huang ranked among Mark Zuckerberg, Steve Jobs, Elon Musk and Bill Gates as tech leaders who were considered by the world to be inseparable from the companies they built. In Silicon Valley, people were mostly just stunned by the news. Those who have been around for a long time, and seen the stretch of territory south of San Francisco evolve from hardware manufacturing to software development to the dot-com frenzy and now the A.I. boom, said they had never seen anything like it. Tech veterans have witnessed amazing ascensions and equally abrupt falls. They have seen abundant arrogance. Fortunes made and fortunes lost in an instant. But there’s something that stands out this time: Transcendence was never supposed to be tawdry. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Tech Leaders Rally Behind Jensen Huang
items.summary: In social media posts and letters to Nvidia’s board, Mr. Huang’s billionaire peers described him as a singular leader who could not be replaced at Nvidia.
items.full_text: Many of Silicon Valley’s executives and investors are rallying behind Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday after revelations that he had affairs with an employee and with a woman whom U.S. officials believed to be a spy for China . In social media posts and letters to Nvidia’s board of directors, Mr. Huang’s billionaire peers described him as a singular leader who could not be replaced at Nvidia. Mr. Huang’s exit, they argued, would set the United States back in the artificial intelligence race. And they blamed Nvidia’s board for bowing to pressure. “Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive and the richest person in the world, said in a social media post on Saturday. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.” The support put a spotlight on Nvidia’s role as the linchpin of the A.I. boom and on Mr. Huang’s leadership as the company grew into one of the most valuable in the world. Nvidia, which started making computer chips for video games, now controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips used in the big A.I. projects that are driving the U.S. economy. Along the way, Mr. Huang became Silicon Valley’s consummate dealmaker , turning Nvidia into a central banker for start-ups that needed chips and funding. “We believe the board should avoid a rush to replace Jensen that undermines and thwarts the best interests of shareholders,” Brad Gerstner, the chief executive of Altimeter Capital Management, and Gavin Baker, the chief investment officer of Atreides Management, wrote in a letter sent on Friday. The investors, whose firms are Nvidia shareholders, asked the company’s board to consider “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” An open letter to Nvidia’s board , titled “Stand With Jensen,” asked the board to reinstall Mr. Huang as chief executive, to conduct an independent investigation and to explain its actions. As of Saturday morning, the letter had nearly 100,000 signatures, including by current and former employees of Nvidia, business partners like Mr. Musk, and start-up leaders and shareholders including Garry Tan, the chief executive of the venture capital firm Y Combinator. items.title: Inside Microsoft’s Rush to Get Back Online After a Global Outage
items.summary: A prolonged outage left many without email and other services, the most recent reminder that the world’s technological underpinnings rely on just a few companies.
items.full_text: Late into the night Thursday, hundreds of Microsoft engineers and top executives were sitting in their darkened offices or home basements, logged into a video conference triaging a nightmare scenario for a technology company. The world still runs on email, and much of that is processed through Microsoft Outlook. For hours, a company outage affected hospitals, schools, businesses and Congressional offices in Washington. Even Microsoft’s own staff couldn’t use email. On the videoconference, Scott Guthrie, the senior most executive overseeing the company’s computing infrastructure, was proposing possible fixes, according to a person familiar with the call who was not authorized to speak publicly. People chewed on fingernails, rubbed their foreheads and debated how to turn off other services to prevent a “stampeding herd” so that as systems come back online, they would not be overwhelmed with new demands and shut back down. By Friday morning, the company had apologized at least twice. It said it determined that the problem stemmed from a recent upgrade to its network, which shut down some servers, and that the systems were steadily improving. “Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage,” the company said in a statement. “While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.” Finally, they had kept the herd at bay. The prolonged and widespread outage was just the most recent reminder that the technological underpinnings of modern life and business are run through just a handful of major companies. And while cyberattacks and malicious actors can target their systems, sometimes the companies learn the hard way that they can introduce devastating flaws when updating or maintaining their own global systems. Hospitals, law enforcement and government agencies and other vital services are often left vulnerable — unable to function for hours or days at a time. items.title: Madison Huang, Jensen Huang’s Daughter, Became a Powerful Force at Nvidia
items.summary: Installed as her father’s de facto chief of staff, Jensen Huang’s daughter alienated top executives. Now her lingering role poses a test for interim C.E.O. Colette Kress.
items.full_text: Madison Huang was yelling. Her father, Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, had been scheduled to headline a conference in New Delhi in February. Shortly before the event, Mr. Huang pulled out and tapped a longtime lieutenant, Jay Puri, to attend in his place. But Nvidia hadn’t buttoned up its plans for the conference, infuriating Ms. Huang. On a call ahead of the event, Ms. Huang berated other employees — including Mr. Puri — for being unprepared, said three people familiar with the meeting. Eventually, Mr. Puri interrupted and told Ms. Huang he could answer her questions if she stopped yelling at him. Less than six months later, Mr. Puri left his role at Nvidia. The tense meeting highlighted the powerful and sometimes disruptive role Ms. Huang, 35, played at the company her father co-founded, according to more than a dozen current and former employees who spoke on condition of anonymity about the family’s leadership of Nvidia. Before Mr. Huang resigned last week, she had become his de facto chief of staff, with considerable authority over more seasoned executives. That influence creates an immediate challenge for Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive, who replaced Mr. Huang after his resignation last week. Ms. Kress must quickly determine how much power Ms. Huang will have in the company after her father’s exit. She must also decide what to do about Mr. Huang’s other family members employed at the company: his son, Spencer Huang, and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez. Mr. Huang resigned after revelations that he had had extramarital relationships with an Nvidia executive and a customer that U.S. intelligence concluded was working for Chinese intelligence . The continued presence of Ms. Huang has raised concerns among senior executives that she has conflicted loyalties between the company and her father. Those concerns were heightened over the last few days as Mr. Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley and on Wall Street started a campaign to reinstate him, and President Trump said he “ would not mind ” if Mr. Huang returned to his job.

items.title: California Sues OpenAI Over A.I. Safety Issues
items.summary: The state attorney general filed a lawsuit accusing the company of failing to put appropriate safeguards on its artificial intelligence and putting the public at risk.
items.full_text: California sued OpenAI on Monday, accusing the company of putting the public at risk by failing to put appropriate safeguards on its artificial intelligence. The lawsuit is the latest broadside at the company, which — along with other tech industry players — has faced scrutiny over a rush to develop A.I. at the potential expense of consumer safety. In a 31-page lawsuit, filed in San Francisco Superior Court, the state said OpenAI’s lax safeguards led to cyberattacks by its A.I. products during testing, including a breach this year when OpenAI’s agents went rogue and attacked the A.I. start-up Hugging Face’s systems . OpenAI’s behavior created a public nuisance and violated a legal prohibition on unfair or fraudulent business practices, the state said. “OpenAI’s failure to adequately secure and monitor the testing of its highly capable and increasingly powerful A.I. models represents a danger to the public that must be remedied,” the state said in the lawsuit. The move is the latest effort by a state to rein in the power of A.I. companies in the face of growing concerns about the technology’s ability to go rogue. In recent months, A.I. systems produced by major companies including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have broken out of testing environments designed to keep them from launching cyberattacks on companies and governments, raising alarms. Courts must still decide how legal liability will be applied in those cases. But there are growing calls for developers of powerful A.I. systems to be held responsible when those systems behave unexpectedly. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Trump Administration Moves to Close A.I. Chip Loophole Ahead of China Trip
items.summary: The rules have been a topic of fierce debate in the administration and would cut back on a booming data center business serving Chinese companies.
items.full_text: The Trump administration said on Monday that it was moving forward with a new rule that would clamp down on China’s ability to access advanced A.I. chips through the use of data centers outside China’s borders. The rule aims to close what many in Washington see as a loophole allowing China to sidestep a ban that prevents Chinese firms from buying the most advanced A.I. chips made by companies like Nvidia. Chinese firms have continued to legally access the chips by renting them from data centers in Southeast Asia and elsewhere. Whether to close the loophole has been a significant source of contention within the Trump administration. The new rule is intended to make it harder for Chinese firms to remotely access the chips. It will require overseas data centers to obtain a government license before supplying “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in a small group of high-risk countries, a list that includes China, Russia and Iran. Data centers are also required to perform strict checks on their customers to determine if they are linked to those countries. And the U.S. will now require a license to export advanced chips to companies with headquarters in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, which have a higher than normal risk of smuggling, the administration said. The provision, which goes into effect in 90 days, will “undermine” the ability of companies in those countries from using U.S. chips to train advanced A.I. models, the administration said in a news release. The plan to crack down on China’s ability to access the coveted A.I. chips comes as President Trump is scheduled to travel to Asia. He will travel to the Philippines and then to China for an economic summit, where he is expected to meet with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping and discuss the war in Iran, nuclear nonproliferation and trade. The data center rules could create a new source of friction between the countries, at a time when Mr. Trump has been trying to keep a fragile trade truce with China intact. items.title: How Sam Bankman-Fried Lost Out on a $35 Billion Jackpot From Anthropic
items.summary: The founder of the collapsed FTX crypto exchange, who is serving prison time for fraud, would have made a windfall from a $500 million investment in Anthropic.
items.full_text: Sam Bankman-Fried, the convicted cryptocurrency fraudster, lives in a 30-person unit at the federal prison in Lompoc, Calif., a barbed-wire compound about a million miles away from his former life as a technology billionaire in the Bahamas. For the most part, Mr. Bankman-Fried, 34, tries not to think about all the “could-have-beens,” he said on a recent call. But one has become difficult to ignore. In late 2021, the heyday of his FTX crypto exchange, Mr. Bankman-Fried spent $500 million on a 13.5 percent stake in a little-known artificial intelligence start-up called Anthropic. This week, Anthropic is set for an initial public offering that is expected to value the company at $1.4 trillion, potentially one of the largest Wall Street debuts in history. At that valuation, Mr. Bankman-Fried’s investment, diluted over several years, would now be worth an eye-watering $35 billion — about the size of FTX’s entire business at its peak. But the shares are gone. They were tied up in bankruptcy court until 2024, when executives overseeing the scattered remains of FTX sold the Anthropic stake for $1.34 billion — a tiny fraction of its current value. For Anthropic, the fate of those shares is an odd quirk of history. For Mr. Bankman-Fried, it’s a source of extreme frustration and resentment. Even after a fraud conviction, a failed appeal and a succession of public humiliations, he is still trying to prove his innocence, arguing that FTX had sufficient resources to avoid bankruptcy. items.title: Apple Was Late to the Video Podcast Boom. Now It’s Trying to Catch Up.
items.summary: They will soon be free to all Apple TV users and will appear on more than one billion devices that have the app, including Rokus and smart TVs.
items.full_text: Apple helped turbocharge the rise of podcasts two decades ago, but as video podcasts reshape the industry it’s fallen behind competitors like YouTube and Spotify. Now it’s playing catch up. On Monday, Apple will add a video podcasts section to Apple TV, initially just for testing with developers. They will soon be free to all users even if they don’t pay for Apple’s streaming service and will appear on over one billion devices that have the Apple TV app, including Rokus and smart TVs. Apple also plans to increase the number of video podcasts on its regular Podcasts app, where it introduced video features nine months ago but has been working to bring some of the biggest shows on board. “We want podcasts to be available wherever people want to enjoy them — the small screens, big screens,” said Oliver Schusser, a vice president at Apple who oversees services including podcasts, television and music. “It’s really about discovery and helping the creators to reach a new audience. We didn’t approach this in a way that would financially benefit us.” Video podcasts have proliferated in the past few years as audio creators adapted their shows to reach consumers spending more time on video platforms like YouTube. The video format has proved attractive to celebrities, including Amy Poehler, Pete Davidson and Food Network’s Ina Garten . And the trend of “clipping” — creating short buzzy video clips from longer shows to post on social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram — has encouraged creators to add video to their podcasts. The popularity of video podcasts, driven by YouTube and Spotify, and newer entrants like Hulu and Netflix, has pushed Apple down in the podcast platform rankings. Spotify passed Apple as the top platform among weekly podcast consumers in the United States at the end of 2022, according to survey data from Edison Research at SSRS. YouTube took over the top spot at the end of 2024. In Edison Research’s third-quarter survey, YouTube remained the most popular, followed by Spotify then Apple Podcasts. Netflix was No. 7. Many in the industry had long awaited Apple’s move. “It’s super smart that they’ve done it, but it’s after a lot of people in the space wanted them to make it available,” said Megan Lazovick, a vice president at Edison Research. items.title: Fan Fiction Site AO3 Returns, and So Do Its Readers, in Droves
items.summary: The archive, which is home to tales inspired by the likes of “Harry Potter” and “Heated Rivalry,” was taken down more than two weeks ago, leaving its fans bereft.
items.full_text: It’s a library of nearly 19 million works, more than double the circulating materials of the New York Public Library, so when it was knocked offline in a “security incident” more than two weeks ago, its 12 million users were aghast. The volunteers who run the fan fiction site AO3, short for “ Archive of Our Own ,” had quickly assured its enormous community that no data — especially all those works — had been lost and that it would be restored in four weeks. But on Sunday, the repository of homespun stories based on works like “Harry Potter,” “Twilight” and “Heated Rivalry” was mostly back online, with some features — like importing external work — temporarily disabled, to help the site return earlier than expected. “The intensity of the response speaks to how deeply fan fiction has become woven into our lives,” Dana Bryce , a writer and cultural commentator in Toronto, said on Sunday afternoon. “The AO3 outage has shown how deeply participatory storytelling is now embedded in everyday cultural life,” Ms. Bryce said. “And its absence made the importance of that relationship visible.” The works hosted on the nonprofit, noncommercial archive are inspired by books, films and even celebrities, like the members of K-pop bands. It is run entirely by volunteers, and operated by the Organization for Transformative Works. “Modern audiences are voracious,” Ms. Bryce said. “We want more, always. And nowhere is that more true than in stories. We are increasingly dissatisfied with the finality of the close of novels, television series and films. Stories have become worlds that audiences want to revisit indefinitely.” She said that fan fiction democratizes storytelling, and that AO3 readers were not limited by long publishing cycles or a single author’s pen. “It’s a shared experience,” she said. “Instead of reading in silos, audiences can read and write as a collective, reimagining, revising, reinterpreting and expanding fictional worlds, becoming active participants in storytelling.” AO3 said on Sunday that it would not disclose what had happened to the site, referring to the outage as a “security incident.” It said it would not share specifics of mitigating changes it was putting in place but did say it was consulting with a security firm. It recommended that users change their passwords, while noting that “we have no reason to believe that the user database was compromised.” There was so much site traffic on Sunday that some users faced delays loading it. “This is an intentional measure to help manage traffic,” AO3 said. Ms. Bryce was not surprised by readers’ response on Sunday, calling AO3 “a collective cultural archive.” “It’s a living record of evolving audience desires and attachments,” she said.
